title: Persistent public pessimism is converting institutional distrust into demand for disruption, visible results, and affordability
source_unit: FGS Global Radar 2026 public-pessimism report and public findings overview
geography: 27 countries described as major democracies; polling of 20,000 people plus 175 in-depth interviews with global leaders

denominator.unit: countries polled in the FGS Global Radar 2026 frame

pessimism.value: Pessimism is described as the dominant public mood in every country polled

system_failure.unit: percent saying their political system is failing people and requires fundamental reform

elite_gap.unit: percent saying the political system serves rich and powerful elites rather than ordinary working people

legitimacy_route.value: Institutional legitimacy is increasingly judged through lived results, fairness, and visible capacity rather than authority or long-term promises alone

observations.method: FGS Global public overview of polling of 20,000 people across major democracies and 175 in-depth interviews with global leaders; full report methodology is not reproduced on the public findings page.
observations.uncertainty: This is a publisher-produced public-affairs report; the public overview does not provide full country samples, field dates, weighting, question wording, or causal identification. The findings describe sentiment and interpretation, not institutional performance directly.
observations.subgroup: Voters and publics in advanced democracies, leaders and experts, people facing affordability pressure, and groups evaluating whether democratic institutions deliver meaningful change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Pessimism may motivate reform, participation, or accountability rather than only anti-system politics; perceived system failure can also reflect high expectations rather than uniformly worsening outcomes.

denominator.unit: people included in the FGS Global Radar polling frame

strong_leader_rule_breaking.unit: percent saying strong leaders should be willing to break rules to get things done

disruptor_support.value: The report interprets admiration for disruptors as a belief that disruption may be the only way to force change

populism_route.value: Populism is framed as a structural condition sustained by impatience with conventional institutions, not merely a temporary protest vote

observations.method: Descriptive polling summary and qualitative interpretation from the FGS Global Radar 2026 overview, supplemented by leader interviews.
observations.uncertainty: The association between pessimism and support for rule-breaking leaders is not a causal estimate; the public page does not show subgroup models, country variation, or whether respondents mean legal exceptions, procedural speed, or authoritarian power.
observations.subgroup: People frustrated with slow or unresponsive institutions, voters attracted to outsider candidates, and publics weighing procedural safeguards against immediate results.
observations.counterinterpretation: Demand for disruption may mean administrative reform, anti-corruption action, or faster implementation within democratic rules rather than rejection of democracy itself.

observations.period: 2026; elite expectations, taxation, and policy trade-offs

denominator.unit: people included in the FGS Global Radar polling frame

competent_government_without_tax_increas.unit: percent believing a competent government could meet public expectations without raising taxes

expert_public_gap.value: Policies experts describe as necessary or inevitable are often rejected by publics who expect better outcomes without accepting visible trade-offs

complexity_penalty.value: In a distrustful environment, technical complexity can be interpreted as deflection and caution as unwillingness to act

observations.method: FGS Global polling and expert-interview synthesis concerning public expectations, government competence, taxes, spending, AI, and economic reform.
observations.uncertainty: The result does not measure fiscal literacy, policy alternatives, actual tax incidence, or whether respondents would accept specific trade-offs when described concretely.
observations.subgroup: Taxpayers, voters, policymakers, consumers facing cost pressure, and publics judging whether economic policy distributes burdens fairly.
observations.counterinterpretation: The finding may reflect distrust in current spending or tax administration rather than an impossible belief that public services have no resource constraints.

observations.period: 2026; affordability and fairness as legitimacy signals

affordability.value: Affordability is identified as central to regulatory decisions, political strategy, and consumer behavior

fairness.value: Fairness is treated as a legitimacy condition rather than a peripheral policy preference

near_term_results.value: Messages relying on institutional authority, technical expertise, or long-term promises struggle unless they address lived experience and near-term impact

observations.method: Publisher synthesis of public polling and leader interviews across politics, business, technology, and society.
observations.uncertainty: This is a strategic synthesis rather than an independently specified causal model; affordability and fairness may be causes, outcomes, or interpretive lenses for broader distrust.
observations.subgroup: Households and consumers under cost pressure, voters evaluating economic policy, regulators, firms, and institutions seeking legitimacy across polarized publics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Near-term delivery can build trust but may also reward short-termism, weaken investment in long-horizon public goods, or encourage symbolic action over durable capacity.

related_sources.claim: Official public findings overview for sample frame, public pessimism, institutional reform, disruptor support, elite perceptions, and affordability/fairness interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a global public-pessimism and legitimacy layer connecting institutional distrust to disruption, political impatience, affordability, fairness, and consumer behavior. It is a publisher-produced polling and interview synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a representative global census, a causal model of populism, proof that institutions are objectively failing, or evidence that rule-breaking leadership improves outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official FGS Global Radar 2026 public findings page reviewed for the 27-country frame, 20,000-person polling description, 175 leader interviews, pessimism, reform, rule-breaking leadership, elite-service perceptions, competent-government expectations, and affordability/fairness findings.
